name: Game Theory
description: A lens for composing Factors from the language of strategic interactions, decisions, and equilibria. Maps game-theoretic concepts—players, strategies, payoffs, Nash equilibrium, extensive and normal forms, cooperative games, and evolutionary dynamics—to the 19-node topology. Useful for Factors involving competition, cooperation, bargaining, and strategic decision-making.

x.note: The depth anchor—the number of players in the game. Part of the 4‑cycle x→a→9→y→x, linking player count to strategy space, information sets, and information structure.

y.note: The relational anchor—information available to players (complete/incomplete, perfect/imperfect). Part of the 4‑cycle x→a→9→y→x, tying information to player count, strategy space, and decision points.

z.note: The transformational anchor—temporal dimension (one‑shot vs repeated). Persistently connected to 0 (player), reflecting that repeated play depends on the player’s perspective.

0.note: The point of observation—a player in the game. Persistently connected to z (time), linking the player to repeated interactions.

1.note: The boundary—the complete specification of players, strategies, payoffs, and information. Part of the 4‑cycle 1→6→5→2→1, connecting game boundaries to equilibria, game forms, and strategies.

2.note: Primitive—a pure strategy or action. Completes the 1‑6‑5‑2 cycle, showing how strategies are embedded in game boundaries, equilibria, and game forms.

3.note: The invariant law—mapping from strategy profiles to payoffs. A node in the 7‑core; connected to best response (c) and learning (e), as payoffs define best responses and shape learning dynamics.

4.note: The fundamental relation—selection of strategies by players. A node in the 7‑core; connected to randomness (b) and equilibrium set (f), as play involves chance and leads to equilibrium.

5.note: The pattern—extensive form representation: nodes, branches, information sets. Part of the 1‑6‑5‑2 cycle, bridging equilibria and strategies.

6.note: The transformation—strategy profile where no player can unilaterally improve. Part of the 1‑6‑5‑2 cycle, connecting game boundaries to game forms.

7.note: The realization—actual strategies chosen in an instance. Persistently connected to 8 (strategy space size), linking the outcome to the complexity of the strategy space.

8.interpretation: Quantization / Strategy Space Size / Payoff Resolution
8.note: The granularity—number of pure strategies or payoff granularity. Persistently connected to 7 (outcome), reflecting that the size of the strategy space determines possible outcomes.

9.note: The event—a decision point in the game. Part of the 4‑cycle x→a→9→y→x, placing decision points between strategy space, player count, and information structure.

a.note: Pure potential—Cartesian product of all players' strategy sets. Initiates the 4‑cycle x→a→9→y→x, linking strategy space to player count, information sets, and information structure.

b.note: The arena—introduction of chance: mixed strategies, nature’s moves. A node in the 7‑core; connected to interaction (4) and memory (d), as randomness affects play and can be remembered.

c.note: Directional bias—tendency to choose strategies that maximize payoff. A node in the 7‑core; connected to payoff function (3) and equilibrium set (f), as best responses are derived from payoffs and lead to equilibrium.

d.note: Persistent structure—record of past actions in repeated games. A node in the 7‑core; connected to randomness (b) and equilibrium set (f), as memory of chance outcomes shapes equilibrium in repeated games.

e.note: The active algorithm—process by which strategies evolve or beliefs update. A node in the 7‑core; connected to payoff function (3) and equilibrium set (f), as learning is driven by payoffs and converges to equilibrium.

f.note: The resonant cavity—the set of all equilibria or the socially optimal outcome. A node in the 7‑core; connected to interaction (4), best response (c), memory (d), learning (e), and payoff function (3), forming the central hub of strategic outcomes.

values.n=2: 2‑player — classic game theory (Prisoner's Dilemma, Battle of Sexes)

values.m=3: Very complex — extensive trees, repeated games
values.m=4: Extreme — infinite strategy spaces, Bayesian games

m.formula: m = floor(log₂(|S|)) where |S| is the number of pure strategy profiles

phase.formula: φ = e^{2πi × (cooperative index)} where cooperative index is the fraction of maximum possible total payoff achieved
phase.special: Phase = 0 for pure defection, phase = π for full cooperation, phase = π/2 for mixed outcomes
phase.significance: Phase encodes the degree of cooperation or the relative payoff in a bargaining solution.

normal_form.description: The Factor viewed as a matrix (payoff table) with players, strategies, and payoffs

extensive_form.description: The Factor viewed as a game tree with nodes, branches, and information sets
extensive_form.phase_condition: Phase as the branch angle or information set index

evolutionary.description: The Factor viewed as a population dynamics (replicator, Moran process)
evolutionary.phase_condition: Phase as the frequency of a strategy in the population

cooperative.description: The Factor viewed as a cooperative game with coalitions and characteristic function
cooperative.phase_condition: Phase as the Shapley value share or bargaining power

creating_anew.note: When creating a game, start with players (node 0) and their strategies (node 2). Define the payoff function (node 3) and the game form (node 5). Compute equilibria (node 6) and analyze outcomes (node 7).

translating_known.prisoners_dilemma: Map to node 1 as 2×2 normal form, node 3 as payoff matrix, node 6 as (Defect,Defect) equilibrium, node φ as 0 (defection)
translating_known.ultimatum_game: Map to node 5 as extensive tree, node 0 as proposer and responder, node 9 as decision nodes, node 6 as subgame perfect equilibrium
translating_known.rock_paper_scissors: Map to node 2 as three strategies, node 3 as cyclic payoffs, node 6 as mixed equilibrium, node b as mixed strategy
translating_known.public_goods_game: Map to node 2 as contribute/defect, node d as history in repeated version, node e as learning dynamics

temporary_note.special: Players and their strategy sets defined, but payoff matrix not yet specified. Awaiting utility assignments.

constraints.rationality: Players aim to maximize their own payoff; preferences are transitive and complete.
constraints.equilibrium_consistency: In a Nash equilibrium, no player can gain by unilaterally deviating; this must hold for node 6.
constraints.information_consistency: Information sets (node 9) must be consistent: players cannot distinguish between nodes in the same information set.
constraints.stratum_preference: global for general game theory; trefoil_g for evolutionary and learning games; trefoil_c for cooperative and axiomatic games; fig8 for games with incomplete information (Harsanyi transformation).
constraints.invariant_core: The Game Theory paradigm respects the persistent skeleton from trefoil_i, which decomposes into five subsystems: (1) edge 0→z linking player to repeated interaction, (2) edge 8→7 linking strategy space size to realized outcome, (3) 4‑cycle x→a→9→y→x linking player count–strategy space–information set–information structure, (4) 4‑cycle 1→6→5→2→1 linking game boundaries–equilibrium–game form–strategy, and (5) 7‑node core {3,4,b,c,d,e,f} encoding the heart of game theory: payoff function–interaction–randomness–best response–memory–learning–equilibrium set.
